evals.name: mym-budget-debt
evals.prompt: Using the Consumer Reports Complete Guide to Managing Your Money, help me set up a household budget. I have about $9,000 in credit card and car loan debt and no savings, and I want to start investing in stocks. What does the book say I should do, in what order?
assertions: Describes the book's four budgeting steps: cash-flow analysis, setting budget goals, allocating resources, and a year-end review
Recommends building an emergency fund before investing
Cites the book's guideline that monthly debt payments excluding the mortgage should not exceed 15 percent of gross income
States the book says not to invest in stocks until debts are under control and insurance is adequate
Notes the book is from 1989 and flags that some figures/rules are outdated or should be verified
Gives a clear ordered action plan (track cash flow, pay high-interest debt, emergency fund, insurance, then invest)

evals.name: mym-life-insurance
evals.prompt: I'm 34, married with two young kids. According to the Consumer Reports money guide, how should I figure out how much life insurance I need, and what kind should I buy? Is credit life insurance on my car loan worth it?
assertions: Explains the book's three-step method: estimate family expenses if you die (immediate and future), subtract assets/income sources, insure the gap
Says the book considers credit-life insurance usually not a good buy and that one larger policy beats several small ones
Mentions including Social Security survivor benefits, existing savings or spouse income as resources
Recommends or discusses low-cost term coverage for the years dependents need support
Flags that 1989 product details/prices are dated and suggests verifying current quotes

evals.name: mym-credit-denied
evals.prompt: I was just turned down for a credit card. What does the Consumer Reports Complete Guide to Managing Your Money say about credit reports and what I should do now? Also, I'm married—does that affect my credit file?
assertions: Explains you are entitled to see your credit bureau file, with the fee waived if denied credit recently (within 30 days per the book)
Advises reviewing the report and disputing errors
Mentions the Equal Credit Opportunity Act 'user' designation so a married person gets credit for accounts in the spouse's name
Notes many routine payments (rent, utilities, phone, medical) are not reported to credit bureaus
Mentions current free access via annualcreditreport.com and/or FCRA dispute rights as an update to the 1989 book
Mentions skepticism toward paid credit-repair or credit-credential services
